analysis.one_liner: Gives farmers new rights against biotech seed companies, including seed-saving rights and strict company liability.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to three House committees and their subcommittees and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules between farmers and the companies that sell genetically engineered seeds, plants, and animals. It would void seed-contract terms that block farmers from saving seed, bar mandatory arbitration and liability-shifting clauses, cap US technology fees at the prices charged abroad, require written warnings of legal and environmental risks, and make biotech companies strictly liable for injuries caused by their engineered organisms. It would also protect farmers who do not plant engineered crops, by fighting cross-pollination contamination, false non-engineered labels, and lender pressure to buy engineered seed. It died in committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers who buy or avoid genetically engineered seed. They would regain the right to save seed from a harvested crop, keep the ability to sue when seed fails to perform as advertised, be shielded from mandatory arbitration and from granting company agents access to their land, pay no higher technology fees than farmers abroad pay, and be protected from contamination from a neighbor's engineered crops. Non-engineered and organic farmers would gain the most, since contamination can cost them their markets. Consumers would gain from pest-resistance safeguards and honest seed labeling.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farmers, especially non-GE and organic growers

how_it_helps.text: Voids seed-contract provisions that prohibit or charge for saving harvested seed for replanting, limit a farmer's ability to recover damages when seed does not perform as advertised, shift liability to the farmer, require granting company agents access to the farmer's property, or mandate arbitration or a specific court.
Requires biotech companies to give buyers written notice of the legal and environmental risks of using their products, without shifting liability to the farmer.

Bars a company from charging higher technology or royalty fees in the United States than it charges in other countries, and requires it to disclose its fees country by country, with the data published every six months.
Makes a biotech company liable to any party injured by the release of a genetically engineered organism, when the injury results from the engineering, and forbids waiving that liability by contract.

Directs the Agriculture Secretary to identify crops that cross-pollinate easily and issue rules requiring mitigation strategies, and directs EPA to set the best achievable resistance plan for Bt crops, revoke registrations that do not comply, and cut use of pesticides found to be breeding resistant pests.

Prohibits labeling seed as non-genetically engineered if it actually contains engineered material, bans the manufacture and sale of engineered non-fertile (terminator) seeds, and prohibits lenders from discriminating against a producer who refuses to use engineered plants or animals.

analysis.who_pays: Biotech seed and animal companies, such as Monsanto and DuPont Pioneer, would bear the cost: they would lose the contract terms that currently prevent seed saving and route disputes into arbitration, could be sued for crop failures and contamination injuries they currently avoid by contract, would face civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation per day, and might see lower US technology fees if foreign prices were lower.

drawbacks.text: The strict-liability provision reaches any injury 'resulting from' the engineering, which could expose seed companies to lawsuits even where a farmer misused the product, and farmers who currently accept arbitration clauses in exchange for access to the technology would have to renegotiate terms that could come at a higher price.

Capping US technology fees at the level charged in other countries, and requiring disclosure of fees in every market, does not account for differences in development, regulatory, and market costs between countries, and could reduce the companies' incentive to sell in the US market.

The outright ban on genetically engineered non-fertile seeds would eliminate a technology some researchers proposed as a way to keep engineered traits from spreading to neighboring crops, trading one contamination-protection tool for a prohibition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's protections for farmers — seed saving, arbitration bans, fee caps, contamination liability — are real and address practices that were documented in the seed industry at the time. The main costs fall on the biotech companies, not on consumers, though some could be passed into seed prices, and the strict-liability and absolute terminator-seed ban are drawn broadly. On balance the benefits to farmers and the integrity of non-engineered crops outweigh the design flaws, but the flaws are real and an honest supporter would want them tightened.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees, which sent pieces of it to four subcommittees, and no committee ever approved it or brought it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on July 29, 2008, with several original cosponsors.
The House referred it to three committees — Agriculture, Energy and Commerce, and Judiciary — rather than one, which splits a bill's chances among multiple gatekeepers.

Over the following months it was further referred to four subcommittees (Health; Specialty Crops, Rural Development, and Foreign Agriculture; Horticulture and Organic Agriculture; and Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry).
No committee reported the bill and no floor vote ever occurred before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, so the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The biotech seed companies are better off: they kept the seed-contract terms, US fee structure, and limits on liability that the bill would have taken away, and no farmer protections were enacted in their place.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and no vote was ever held to test the chamber's split.

industries.note: The bill would void the contract terms these companies use to prevent seed saving and route disputes into arbitration, cap their US technology fees at foreign price levels, and make them strictly liable for injuries from their engineered organisms. Their gain under the status quo comes from terms farmers cannot negotiate away, so their interest runs against the farmers' here.

Cross-pollination from a neighbor's engineered crop can cost these farmers their premium markets; the bill's mitigation rules, false-labeling ban, and liability for contamination directly protect them.
They would regain seed-saving rights, the right to sue for non-performance, and protection from fee discrimination, at the price of whatever the companies charge to offset the new terms.
